The subject is a turntable rendered in a stock 3D look: a plain box plinth, a simple tonearm made of rectangular primitives, a flat red label, no material storytelling. It reads like a hobbyist Blender scene.
Volumetric god-rays with floating dust are the only 'idea'. This is an effect with no subject; the same orange haze and spotlight cone repeat across every frame.

The title 'ORRERY' is set in a default heavy grotesk and pasted into a glowing disc. There is no typographic relationship to the name, which is an orrery and not a record player, nor any scale or craft.
Compositions are awkward: a near-empty frame showing just a pin on a red edge, inconsistent framing and aspect between shots, and a stiff dolly feel with no choreography or payoff.
Molten gold and metal grow into a crown. The material process itself is the metaphor for how the throne is made.
Real low-key light: specular highlights pick out a cast, pitted metal surface with smoke and depth in the frame.
A classical wide-tracked serif (Trajan-like) is used for the credits and placed against the forms, off-centre and in varied positions. It is not centred like a slide.
The palette is held to bronze, black and cold silver, which suits monarchy and stays restrained.
The frames move from macro abstraction to faceted jewels to the title reveal, so there is clear choreography.
gaps: The idea is close to a genre convention for prestige drama (macro liquid metal against black). B's world-building concept is more distinctive.
Several frames read as a dark ground with a small tracked-caps credit. That gives less range in composition and scale than B.
The end title is a plain centred serif on a dark haze, without the integrated object or emblem that B's lock-up has.

tells: It has a specific idea that only this piece could have: a clockwork map of the world whose cities mechanically build themselves. This is an orientation device and a memorable image at once.
The material is dense and tactile: carved, engraved bands, brass gears, aged map textures and wood.
Sun-bleached flare and an armillary light source motivate the light and tie the frames together.
Credits carry house sigils in a custom-feeling inscriptional face, and they are integrated into the world.
Each frame is a different scale and vantage (macro band, aerial city, mechanism close-up, top-down map, emblem), which implies strong camera choreography.
The title lock-up is built into the sculpted dragon emblem.
gaps: The warm sepia grade flattens some frames, so the map frame reads a little muddy.
The credit type is small and sometimes fights the busy textures (the Michelle Fairley credit sits against detail).
The bloom on the final title leans toward overexposure cliché.

tells: The 3D is surreal and organic: translucent hands, coral-like growths, hair, fibre and mesh. These are custom simulations, not stock primitives.
The palette changes deliberately frame to frame (blush, violet dusk, cyan sky, chartreuse, bottle green) while staying coherent.
The materials are rich, with subsurface scattering, glass, textile weave and fur, and the lighting is studio-grade.
Each frame is a strong poster with layered depth (the dense textile frame and the knotted glass tubes).
Its use of the festival's contributor-name format (OFFF MX wordmark, studio names) fits a festival-titles brief.
gaps: The typography is minimal and slide-like: small bold sans names placed upper-left, not integrated with the forms.
The frames read as a showcase of disconnected vignettes, not one through-line idea. A unifying concept would lift it toward B.
The type and image need clearer choreography between frames, such as transitions that morph one organism into the next.

tells: A single strong idea: molten gold being cast into the crown, so the title sequence shows the forging of the monarchy itself
Real material rendering: liquid metal, pitted gold surface, faceted gems with caustic highlights, smoky low-key light
Restrained engraved-style spaced serif credits placed off-centre and set against the image, so the type works with the frame instead of sitting on it like a slide
Macro framing changes from shot to shot (wide smoke, horizontal pour, diagonal close-up, top-down gem setting) and builds to the reveal
Its risk is that the dark ground, tracked serif and empty end card come close to the 'tasteful' cliché. What saves it is the material work and the narrative build
gaps: The final title card is a plain centred serif on a dark gradient. It needs the integration of image and type that B's logo lockup has
The near-monochrome black and gold lacks the palette range and environmental world-building B achieves
The credits are elegant but timid. One expressive typographic moment would lift it above 'beautiful but expected'

tells: An idea only this show could have: a mechanical clockwork map where the world builds itself, which also works as a weekly orientation device for viewers
A dense, layered world: carved astrolabe band, cog-driven cities, Winterfell's tree mechanism, a parchment map with hand-drawn rivers and settlement marks
Choreography is evident across frames: the camera travels across the map, structures unfold, and the sequence moves from a burst of light through the city models to the emblem
Type has a point of view: house sigil icons sit beside small-caps credits, and the custom title lockup is built into the carved dragon emblem
Warm sun-flare light against tactile wood, brass and parchment gives real materiality
gaps: The credit type sometimes sits uneasily over busy detail (e.g. over the bone-tree mechanism), so legibility suffers
The end-card sunburst flare is slightly overcooked compared with the restraint elsewhere
The palette leans toward a uniform warm sepia grade. More colour contrast between regions would sharpen the storytelling

tells: A deliberate, unusual palette: dusty rose, clinical blue, acid green and chrome against organic flesh tones
Rich hybrid materials: translucent rubbery hands, mesh, fur and fibres, glass-and-chrome tubes, sculpted terrain, which shows real look-dev effort
Every frame is a different world (pink dusk, volcanic night, studio blue, macro thicket, green ring knot), which suggests a festival or conference opener with contributing studios
The typography is weak: bold-grotesk names sit in the top-left like labels, and only the custom OFFF-style mark shows any typographic idea
It reads as a showcase of renders rather than one through-line idea, and the hand and tentacle organic-surreal look is a trend of the moment
gaps: It lacks a single unifying concept. The vignettes don't build to anything the way B's map builds to its emblem
Type is placed like captions in default bold sans. It needs integration and scale contrast with the 3D
There is no choreographic continuity between frames, so it feels like cuts between separate pieces rather than one designed film

tells: Festival-ident structure: each frame is a different collaborator's world (Boldtron, Medusa Lab), with a festival lockup (OFFF MX) tying them together. That is a curated, multi-studio commission, not a template.

Dense, layered material work: translucent jelly hands holding a flesh-coral heart, knitted mesh and ribbed fabric folds with fibres, glassy organic sculptures, a beaded cluster caught in glossy tubes. Every frame has tactile surface detail.
Unusual palettes chosen per scene: dusty pink over rust terrain, pistachio and blush, bottle-green with ice-blue. These are confident choices, not one accent on a dark ground.
Strong variety between frames: macro organic abstraction, a volcanic landscape, a sculpture against the sky. The piece builds a surreal 'bodies and terrain' theme rather than repeating one layout.
gaps: The typography is mostly small studio-name tags in a generic heavy grotesk dropped into a corner. Unlike B, the type is never integrated into the image or the world.
The cohesion is thematic rather than choreographed. The frames read as a compilation of separate pieces, with no clear camera path or single conceptual journey like B's travelling map.
The idea is strong as a mood but less specific. Push one governing concept, such as a body that becomes the landscape, so the piece is about something memorable as well as showcasing materials.

tells: A specific idea that only this piece could have: the world is rendered as a mechanical, clockwork map, and cities grow out of it like a tabletop orrery. The titles double as geography exposition.

Clear choreography between frames: the astrolabe band opens on sun-flare, the camera swoops over cogwork cities, a bird's-eye shot locates King's Landing on the parchment map, and the band's emblem returns as the logo lockup. The sequence is bookended and continuous.
Real material and light: tooled leather or bronze relief, aged wood and metal miniatures, a parchment map with ink rivers, a warm sun burst against a cool, murky world.
Typography belongs to the world: small trajan-like credit caps with a house sigil beside each name, set low in the frame so the image leads, and a metal-relief title with dragons on the lockup.
gaps: This is the benchmark entry. The credit type is very small and sometimes sits on busy detail ('Michelle Fairley' over the city), which costs legibility.
The palette is a fairly conventional fantasy one: amber flare, sepia and verdigris. A more surprising colour decision would make it unimpeachable.
The logo lockup leans on a familiar sun-burst and lens-flare gesture that is less inventive than the mechanical world before it.

tells: Macro photography, or a very convincing render, of molten and cast gold forming the crown. The concept is metal being shaped into the crown, a quiet metaphor for power being forged.
Light is genuinely crafted: specular glints on rough gold, smoky darkness, gemstone facets with real refraction and shallow depth of field. The texture serves the subject.
Credits use classic small-caps spacing and are placed off-centre in negative space, varied from frame to frame. The final 'THE CROWN' lockup is restrained in a Trajan-like serif.
The macro framings vary (diagonal, horizontal, corner), which implies a slow, weighty and deliberate camera.
gaps: The dark ground with a centred, tracked serif title is close to the genre default for prestige-drama titles. The end card on its own could be mistaken for a template.
The palette stays narrowly in gold on black, so the frames blur together. B, by contrast, moves between sun, stone, map and metal.
The idea is a single process shot with no narrative or geographical layer. Adding a second element, such as history or individuals carved into the metal, would give it the specificity of B.

defects: Unresolved path-tracing or volumetric noise in the haze (shots 2–4): the beam crawls with speckle that reads as render noise, not film grain or dust
Tonearm and plinth geometry is simple and soft-edged (headshell is a plain box, chrome has no fine bevels or highlights), so it doesn't hold up at the close framings it is given
Product details don't match between shots: the tonearm shape, the plinth's depth and the label all change from the wide shot to the close-ups
Label type on the record is soft and smeared in the crop; 'ORRERY' sits on a blown-out disc with no detail in the highlight
The end frame crowds the logo disc against a cropped turntable in the lower left, so the two shapes compete
Shot 3 (soft tonearm rising out of frame, empty amber wall) holds roughly 1 s on almost nothing: dead air
The music bed is cut off sharply at about 19.5 kHz, which suggests a lossy or library source rather than a mix built for this piece
gaps: Motion is slow dollies plus one tonearm drop, with no mechanical weight: the stylus doesn't settle or bounce on contact and the platter has no visible spin-up. The orbiting dust, the one idea that could carry the 'orrery' name, only appears in the wide shot instead of building across the whole piece

Sound is four isolated ticks, a gap, then a dense bed dropping in at 6.4 s with scattered transients and a quick tail. There is no designed needle-drop, vinyl crackle or room tone, and the drop is not prepared for. Little in it is built to match the picture

Finish is below studio level: noisy volumetrics, simple chrome shading, an inconsistent product model and a soft, overexposed logo end card. Top studios would denoise the haze, add micro-detail to the hero object and design a lockup that rhymes with the opening light source
